TextView.android:text: Intermediate Lesson 9: Graph Theory & Advanced Pigeonhole

A 'Graph' is a set of Vertices (points) connected by Edges (lines). The 'Degree' of a vertex is the number of edges connected to it. 
The Handshake Lemma is the most fundamental theorem in graph theory: The sum of the degrees of all vertices in a graph is exactly twice the number of edges.
∑ deg(v) = 2E. 
A direct consequence: In any graph, the number of vertices with an ODD degree must be EVEN. You can never have exactly 3 people in a room who have each shaken hands an odd number of times.

Can you draw a shape without lifting your pen and without tracing the same line twice? This is the problem of Eulerian paths.
• Eulerian Circuit (starts and ends at the SAME vertex): Exists if and only if EVERY vertex in the connected graph has an EVEN degree.
• Eulerian Path (starts and ends at DIFFERENT vertices): Exists if and only if exactly TWO vertices have an ODD degree. (You must start at one odd vertex and end at the other).
This solves the famous 'Seven Bridges of Königsberg' problem.

We know that if N items are put into K boxes (where N > K), at least one box contains more than one item. \nThe Generalized Version states: If N items are placed into K boxes, at least one box must contain at least ceiling(N/K) items.\nIn Olympiads, the 'boxes' are often abstract. For example, if you pick 5 points inside an equilateral triangle of side length 2, you divide the triangle into 4 smaller triangles (boxes) of side length 1. By the Pigeonhole Principle, at least two points must fall into the same small triangle, proving their distance is ≤ 1.

We saw how 2-coloring (black/white) proved a domino tiling impossible. But some problems require 3-coloring or 4-coloring.\nFor example, if you want to tile a 10x10 board with 1x4 tetrominoes, 2-coloring isn't enough. You color the board with 4 colors (1,2,3,4) in repeating diagonal stripes. Every 1x4 piece will cover exactly one square of each color. If the total number of squares of color 1 does not equal the total squares of color 2 on the board, tiling is impossible.
In a party of 6 people, prove that there are either 3 people who all know each other, or 3 people who are complete strangers to each other. (Friendship is mutual).

Solution: This is the classic Ramsey's Theorem R(3,3)=6. 
Pick one person, let's call him Alex. There are 5 other people. By the Pigeonhole Principle, Alex must either know at least 3 of them, or NOT know at least 3 of them.
Case 1: Alex knows 3 people (B, C, D). If any two of B, C, D know each other (say B and C), then Alex, B, and C form a triangle of friends. If NONE of B, C, D know each other, they form a triangle of strangers. 
Case 2 (Alex doesn't know 3 people) follows the exact same logic but reversed. Thus, it is always guaranteed.
Choose any 51 numbers from the integers 1 to 100. Prove that you must have chosen at least one pair where one number exactly divides the other.

Solution: Every integer can be written in the form (2^k * M), where M is an odd number. 
What are the possible odd numbers (M) between 1 and 100? They are 1, 3, 5, 7... 99. There are exactly 50 odd numbers.
When we pick 51 numbers, we calculate the 'M' value for each of them. Since there are 51 numbers but only 50 possible odd parts, by the Pigeonhole Principle, at least two numbers must share the EXACT SAME odd part (M). 
Let these two numbers be A = 2^x * M and B = 2^y * M. 
Since they share M, if x > y, then B divides A perfectly. If y > x, A divides B perfectly.
